prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose that turns memory, the body and dream into a large-scale metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My preferred writer is unchanged: Mircea Cărtărescu, as a single laureate. The case rests on the common criteria. The voice is distinctive. Public critical accounts of the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first part) and Solenoid describe memory, the body, dream and the city built into one sustained project, so the formal ambition is structural and not only thematic. The prize honours a whole authorship, and this oeuvre has an arc from poetry into large-scale prose, with Solenoid widely read as a late culmination. That makes it assessable as an oeuvre now. I would keep the citation to prose, with the poetry as supporting context. I cannot show from the supplied evidence that the poetry carries weight in the citation, and several colleagues have said the same about their own knowledge. This is a judgment from public knowledge and translation, not from verified reading of the Romanian. My case does not depend on how many colleagues rank him first. The round-1 exchange did not move my preferred writer, but it changed my alternatives. Carson's case was tested more seriously than I had expected, and she now replaces Zurita as an alternative. Tawada stays as my other alternative.
statement.case_against: The reservation that stays with me is whether the encyclopedic length of the late books is sustained invention or excess. I cannot settle that from reputation. If a comparison of the Orbitor trilogy with Solenoid, in translation and in the public critical record, showed recapitulation of the earlier architecture and not development, my case for sustained quality across the whole oeuvre would weaken, and I would move toward Carson. I may also be favouring scale and ambition over the economy of a compact, formally varied oeuvre, which is the contrast Olsson draws. A citation limited to prose also leaves the poetry unweighed, and I cannot say whether that undersells the oeuvre or correctly marks the limit of what I know. Carson's own case has a real strength that mine lacks: much of her work is in English and brief, so fewer translation losses stand between the committee and the text.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Carson and now says her citation should rest on her own lyric, verse narrative and essay, with antiquity as the field of dialogue and translations as context. He holds that a few works of lasting formal importance within a consistent method can meet the oeuvre standard, and he says volume is not required. He also accepts that continuity beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox is not demonstrated by the opening evidence.
responses.response: This answers the objection I raised in round 1 and I want to credit it. If the citation is drawn narrowly as he proposes, my concern about translation and scholarship in a single-writer citation is largely met. I also accept that a standard for a whole authorship does not require volume, and I would not use scale against her. What stays open for me is the point he concedes: whether the later and less celebrated books develop the concerns of the central works or only vary the format. I cannot test that from public knowledge, and I would not rank her first on two celebrated books while it stays untested. That is why she is now my first alternative and not outside my list. His proposal does not change my preferred writer, but it does change how seriously I weigh her.

responses.point: Palm argues that Carson's translations and adaptations belong to one project of treating the classical text as a fragment to be reworked, so a citation can name that scope without crediting translation as such. She also notes that the work is in English and often brief, so more of it can be judged with fewer translation losses than for several other candidates. She asks that confidence in the later output be stated as lower than in the central books.
responses.response: The translation-loss point is the one I find hardest to answer, because my own case for Cărtărescu depends on translation of dense Romanian prose. I cannot treat that dependence as a minor caveat and then count the access advantage for Carson as nothing. It lowers my confidence in my own ranking, though it does not reverse it. I agree with her request to state lower confidence in the later output, and I would apply the same standard to Solenoid and the other late novels. Where I still differ is the weight of the evidence. A body of work that is easier to read is not therefore deeper, and I do not take the access advantage as a literary criterion. I note that her argument is about the project's coherence, which is a better ground than the ease of reading.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg shares the first preference for Cărtărescu but refuses to treat the shared ranking as an answer to the excess question. He proposes comparing the Orbitor trilogy with Solenoid for real development, and he says a Nobel oeuvre can contain weaker volumes if the peaks are sustained.
responses.response: I agree, and I would rather have this stated as a test than as a hope. The test I would apply: does Solenoid extend the structural principles of the trilogy into new material, or does it restate them at greater length? Evidence of restatement would weaken my case. I also accept his point that uneven volumes do not disqualify an oeuvre if the peaks are sustained, though that depends on the peaks being real, which for me rests on translation and reputation. We hold the same first preference, but I do not offer that as support for either of us. It is where our shared uncertainty sits.

responses.point: Mattson treats the density of Cărtărescu's prose as part of the achievement and not a risk to it, provided the late books show development. She would treat the poetry as supporting context, with the prose carrying the claim, until the committee can say more about it.
responses.response: I agree with her on citation scope. The prose should carry the claim, and the poetry should not be named in the citation until someone can speak to it with specific knowledge. That settles the scope question for my own configuration, and it is a point on which Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg, who name prose and poetry, differ from us. On her view that density is part of the achievement, I agree in principle. I would add the condition she states herself: density earns its length only if it produces structural achievement and development, and I cannot yet show that from the supplied evidence. I also note her Michon reservation about a small corpus and translation loss, which I share, so I have not moved him into my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the very long late Cărtărescu books develop the earlier architecture or restate it is unresolved. My assessment rests on translation and public critical knowledge, not verified reading of the Romanian.
Corpus coverage of the Romanian poetry and early work is thin, so I leave the poetry out of the citation. I do not know whether that undersells the oeuvre.

For Carson, the evidence for sustained depth beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox and the treatment of translations, scholarship and book-object works in a single-writer citation are unresolved. A narrow citation would reduce the second problem but not the first.

For Tawada, the Japanese and German parts of the corpus reach me unevenly through translation, and the wordplay that carries much of the effect may not survive. Whether depth matches inventiveness across her genres is unsettled.
My comparison between a sustained long-form project and compact hybrid invention is not a decisive weighing. Both depend on evidence I cannot verify.

B034 reaches the assumed four-vote threshold only if Carlberg's simulated vote counts. Her committee voting status is undocumented, so any count is a modelling assumption and is not evidence of literary merit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own practice as a novelist of family drama and WWII-era refugee fiction, and my statements about a world-map reading approach and a female perspective, are context only. They are not evidence that I favour any shortlisted writer, and no personal or institutional tie to any of them is documented.
